pathophysiology.summary: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is disorganised atrial electrical activity with an irregularly irregular ventricular response. Loss of atrial contraction and fast, irregular ventricular rates reduce cardiac output and cause palpitations, breathlessness and fatigue, and can precipitate heart failure or angina. Stasis in the left atrial appendage allows thrombus to form, so stroke prevention with an oral anticoagulant (OAC) is central to care. The ICMR workflow classifies AF as paroxysmal (under 7 days), persistent (7 days to 1 year), long-standing persistent (over 1 year) or permanent (rate control only). Valvular heart disease, including rheumatic mitral stenosis, remains an important cause in India.
keyMechanisms: Chaotic atrial activation removes the atrial contribution to ventricular filling.
Fast, irregular ventricular rates shorten diastole and lower cardiac output.
Blood stasis in the left atrial appendage forms thrombus that embolises to the brain.
Hypertension, valve disease, heart failure, thyroid disease and alcohol remodel the atria and trigger AF.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm and triage
actions: Confirm AF on a 12-lead ECG (ICMR STW).
Admit if any immediate-intervention indicator: systolic BP below 90 mmHg, rate above 150 or below 50/min, ongoing angina, heart failure, TIA or stroke, or major bleeding on OAC (ICMR STW).
Look for and treat precipitants: thyroid, sepsis, alcohol, pulmonary embolism, ACS (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Haemodynamically unstable
actions: Immediate DC cardioversion after heparinisation (ICMR STW).
Refer to a higher centre if facilities are not available.

clinicalManagement.title: Rate control
actions: Target resting heart rate below 110/min (ICMR STW).
Without heart failure: beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB) — metoprolol, diltiazem or verapamil (ICMR STW).
With heart failure: beta-blocker with digoxin; avoid diltiazem and verapamil in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (ACC/AHA Table 21).

clinicalManagement.title: Stroke prevention
actions: Score CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED; start OAC if CHA2DS2-VASc is above 1 (ICMR STW).
Prefer a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC); use a vitamin K antagonist (VKA) only for severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve, target INR 2–3 (ICMR STW).
Reduce bleeding risk: systolic BP below 140 mmHg; no aspirin, other antiplatelets or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) with OAC; avoid alcohol; correct anaemia (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Rhythm control
actions: Consider for haemodynamic instability, symptoms despite rate control, rate-control side effects or patient preference (ICMR STW).

Drug by substrate (ICMR STW): heart failure — amiodarone; normal heart — flecainide, propafenone, sotalol, amiodarone or ibutilide; coronary disease or LV hypertrophy — amiodarone, sotalol, flecainide or propafenone. Flecainide, propafenone, sotalol and ibutilide are specialist-initiated.
DC cardioversion if drugs fail (ICMR STW).
Consider radiofrequency ablation in selected patients at a tertiary centre (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Referral
actions: Refer if heart rate stays uncontrolled, or with heart failure or angina (ICMR STW).
Reassess OAC need and adequacy at every review (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Stable angina is chest discomfort caused by reversible myocardial ischaemia when oxygen demand on exertion exceeds supply through fixed coronary narrowing. The ICMR workflow defines it as effort-related pain typical of angina that settles with rest or nitroglycerin (NTG) within 1–2 minutes. Treatment has two aims: relieve symptoms with anti-ischaemic drugs, and prevent myocardial infarction and death with an antiplatelet, a high-intensity statin and risk-factor control. Patients whose angina is not controlled on optimal medical therapy, or who are high risk on non-invasive testing, are referred for angiography and possible revascularisation.
keyMechanisms: Fixed atherosclerotic narrowing limits coronary flow reserve.
Exertion, meals, anaemia or tachycardia raise demand beyond supply, causing ischaemic pain.
Rest or nitrates lower demand and preload, relieving pain within minutes.
Plaque rupture converts stable angina into an acute coronary syndrome (ACS).

symptoms: Diffuse retrosternal heaviness or constriction radiating to arms, neck or back
Sweating; reproduced by exertion, especially after meals
Atypical: exertional fatigue, breathlessness, profuse sweating or epigastric discomfort (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Often normal examination
Look for anaemia, hypertension, valve murmurs, heart failure and thyroid signs (contributing factors, ICMR STW)
redFlags: Angina at rest or lasting over 20 minutes (ACS — use the ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) or non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) pathway; ICMR STW)
Recent worsening (crescendo) to Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) class III (ICMR STW)
New effort angina under 1 month, CCS class II or III (ICMR STW)
Post-infarction angina (ICMR STW)
Cardiac arrest survivor or documented ventricular tachycardia (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, febrile illness (ICMR STW)
Uncontrolled hypertension, tachy- or brady-arrhythmias (ICMR STW)

clinicalManagement.title: Primary health centre / community health centre
actions: Exclude ACS: rest pain, pain over 20 minutes, crescendo or new angina go to the STEMI or NSTEMI pathway (ICMR STW).
Control angina with metoprolol, with or without a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB); add a nitrate if not controlled (ICMR STW).
Start aspirin and a high-intensity statin; ECG; refer electively (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: District hospital
actions: Optimise anti-anginal therapy; echocardiography (ICMR STW).
Exercise treadmill test with Duke score if ambulatory with interpretable ECG (ICMR STW).
Angina uncontrolled on optimal medical therapy, abnormal echo, non-ambulatory or uninterpretable ECG, or high-risk stress test (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Tertiary centre
actions: Reassess drugs; if uncontrolled add trimetazidine, nicorandil or ranolazine (ICMR STW).
Risk-stratify with CT coronary angiography, stress imaging or treadmill test (ICMR STW).
Angiography if angina uncontrolled, high-risk non-invasive result, cardiac arrest survivor or documented ventricular tachycardia (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Revascularisation
actions: Revascularise if anatomy is suitable; complete revascularisation preferred (ICMR STW).
Prefer coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) over percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in diabetes with multivessel or left main disease (ICMR STW).
Dual antiplatelet therapy for at least 6 months after PCI (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Contributing factors and prevention
actions: Treat anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, hypertension, heart failure and arrhythmias (ICMR STW).
Secondary prevention: statin, beta-blocker, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Severe hypertension is a BP of 180 mmHg systolic or more and/or 120 mmHg diastolic or more. When it comes with acute damage to the brain, eyes, heart, aorta or kidneys it is a hypertensive emergency and needs controlled IV lowering in a monitored bed. Without acute organ damage, it is treated with oral drugs and lowered gradually over 24–48 hours; IV drugs and rapid falls are avoided because cerebral, coronary and renal autoregulation has shifted upward and a sudden drop can cause ischaemia (ICMR STW; MSD).
keyMechanisms: Abrupt rise in vascular resistance overwhelms autoregulation and injures arteriolar walls.
Endothelial damage causes fibrinoid necrosis, retinal haemorrhages, papilloedema and acute kidney injury.
Raised afterload causes acute left ventricular (LV) failure, pulmonary oedema and myocardial ischaemia.
Chronic hypertension shifts autoregulation upward, so rapid normalisation risks brain, heart and kidney ischaemia.

clinicalManagement.title: Triage
actions: Confirm BP 180/120 mmHg or more on repeat measurement.
Look for symptoms of target-organ damage: visual disturbance, confusion, headache, chest pain, breathlessness, weakness or speech difficulty (ICMR STW).
Symptoms present: stabilise airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) and refer to emergency care at a higher centre (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Hypertensive emergency (higher centre)
actions: Monitored bed with intra-arterial or frequent BP checks.
IV drug chosen by organ involved; reduce mean arterial pressure by 20–25% over about 1–2 hours, then titrate to symptoms (MSD).
Labetalol for most emergencies except acute LV failure; nicardipine for most except acute heart failure; esmolol for aortic dissection; nitroglycerin for myocardial ischaemia or heart failure (MSD).
Do not give oral short-acting nifedipine (MSD).

clinicalManagement.title: Severe hypertension without acute organ damage
actions: Start oral antihypertensives; do not use IV medicines (ICMR STW).
Lower BP gradually over 24–48 hours (ICMR STW).
Refer or admit if symptoms or organ damage are suspected (ICMR STW).
Treat pain or anxiety, which commonly raise readings (MSD).

clinicalManagement.title: Follow-up
actions: Review within 1 week (ICMR STW).
Step up every 4 weeks using the ICMR protocol (amlodipine, then telmisartan, then chlorthalidone) until under 140/90 mmHg (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Acute respiratory failure is failure of the lungs to keep oxygen up (hypoxaemia) or carbon dioxide down (hypercapnia). The ICMR workflow defines hypoxia as SpO2 below 90% and covers the common causes: acute severe asthma, acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), pneumonia, heart failure and pulmonary embolism. Management rests on oxygen titrated to a target, treatment of the cause, and early recognition of patients who need NIV or invasive ventilation. Patients at risk of hypercapnia (COPD, obesity, neuromuscular or chest-wall disease) need a lower SpO2 target of 88–92% because excess oxygen worsens carbon dioxide retention (BTS).
keyMechanisms: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch and shunt (pneumonia, pulmonary oedema) cause hypoxaemia.
Airflow obstruction, fatigue or weak respiratory muscles reduce ventilation and raise PaCO2.
Rising PaCO2 causes respiratory acidosis, drowsiness and asterixis.
Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen in at-risk patients worsens hypercapnia.

clinicalManagement.title: Oxygen
actions: Start oxygen when SpO2 is below 90%; monitor SpO2 and adjust flow (ICMR STW).
Devices: nasal cannula, simple face mask, Venturi mask or non-rebreather mask (ICMR STW).
Target 94–98%, or 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnia (BTS 2017).
Check an ABG in drowsy patients and those at risk of hypercapnia.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat the cause
actions: Bronchodilators for asthma and COPD; steroids; diuretic for heart failure; antibiotics for pneumonia; anticoagulation for suspected pulmonary embolism (ICMR STW).
Pulmonary embolism with high suspicion and low bleeding risk: start low molecular weight heparin, or unfractionated heparin if thrombolysis is anticipated (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Non-invasive ventilation
actions: Start NIV if pH stays below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 6.5 kPa despite optimal therapy (BTS/ICS Rec. 25).
Keep SpO2 88–92% on NIV; optimise settings before raising oxygen (BTS/ICS Recs 4, 23).
Severe acidosis alone does not rule out an NIV trial where intubation is available (BTS/ICS Rec. 26).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation and transfer
actions: Intubate if acidosis persists or worsens on optimised NIV, in respiratory arrest or peri-arrest, or if no interface fits (BTS/ICS Recs 32–34).
Refer if no relief, need for mechanical ventilation or life-threatening features; stabilise circulation, airway and breathing before transfer (ICMR STW).
Continue oxygen and nebulisation during transfer (ICMR COPD STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Acute appendicitis is inflammation of the vermiform appendix, usually from luminal obstruction by a faecolith or lymphoid hyperplasia. Obstruction raises intraluminal pressure, causes ischaemia and bacterial invasion, and if untreated leads to gangrene, perforation, an appendicular mass (phlegmon) or abscess, or generalised peritonitis. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by blood counts and ultrasound (ICMR STW). Appendicectomy, open or laparoscopic, is the standard treatment; patients presenting late with a mass are treated conservatively first (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Luminal obstruction raises pressure in the appendix and impairs venous drainage.
Visceral pain is felt periumbilically, then shifts to the right iliac fossa (RIF) when the parietal peritoneum is involved.
Ischaemia and bacterial invasion cause gangrene and perforation.
Omentum and bowel wall off a perforation to form a mass or abscess; failure causes peritonitis.

symptoms: Periumbilical or epigastric colic shifting to the RIF (ICMR STW)
Nausea or vomiting after the pain starts (ICMR STW)
Loss of appetite (ICMR STW)
Low-grade fever, usually absent in the first 6 hours (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Tenderness at McBurney's point; RIF guarding; rebound tenderness (ICMR STW)
Rovsing's sign, pointing sign, positive cough test (ICMR STW)
Pelvic appendix: cystitis-like symptoms or tenesmus; retrocaecal appendix may mask signs (ICMR STW)
Pregnancy: pain higher in the right flank (ICMR STW)
redFlags: Generalised rigidity: generalised peritonitis (ICMR STW)
Rising pulse or temperature, spreading tenderness, enlarging mass or vomiting during conservative care (ICMR STW stop criteria)
Extremes of age, immunosuppression, diabetes, faecolith, previous abdominal surgery: higher complication risk (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Loin-to-groin pain, haematuria; plain X-ray or ultrasound shows a stone (ICMR STW).
Dysuria, pyuria on urinalysis (ICMR STW).
Dysmenorrhoea, purulent vaginal discharge, bilateral pain (ICMR STW).
Sudden severe epigastric pain; free gas on X-ray (ICMR STW).
Rigors and high fever within 24 hours of pain onset make appendicitis most unlikely (ICMR STW).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Essentially clinical; ultrasound confirms and shows periappendicular collection or abscess; CT if uncertain.

Alvarado below 5 excludes appendicitis (99% sensitivity); high risk: Alvarado 9–10, Appendicitis Inflammatory Response (AIR) 9–12 or Adult Appendicitis Score (AAS) 16 or more. Alvarado should not be used alone to confirm appendicitis in adults (Rec. 1.3).
72 hours or more: no mass — appendicectomy; palpable mass — Ochsner-Sherren conservative regimen.
Laparoscopic appendicectomy within 24 hours of admission for uncomplicated appendicitis (Rec. 3.1–3.2); within 8 hours for complicated appendicitis in children (Rec. 3.3).

pathophysiology.summary: Gallstones form when bile is supersaturated with cholesterol or bilirubin. Most stay silent. A stone impacting in the cystic duct causes biliary colic; persistent obstruction with inflammation becomes acute cholecystitis, which can progress to empyema, gangrene, perforation or mucocele. Stones passing into the common bile duct cause obstructive jaundice, cholangitis or acute pancreatitis. Ultrasound is the investigation of choice (sensitivity 95%, ICMR STW) and laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment.
keyMechanisms: Cholesterol or pigment supersaturation and gallbladder stasis form stones.
Transient cystic duct obstruction causes biliary colic.
Persistent obstruction with chemical then bacterial inflammation causes acute cholecystitis.
Duct stones cause jaundice, cholangitis or pancreatitis.

symptoms: Biliary colic: constant right upper quadrant (RUQ) or epigastric pain with a crescendo-decrescendo pattern (ICMR STW)
Acute cholecystitis: pain over 24 hours with fever (ICMR STW)

physicalSigns: Murphy's sign; RUQ tenderness or mass (Tokyo local signs)

redFlags: Not looking well, not ambulatory or not tolerating oral intake (ICMR STW)

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Local signs (Murphy's sign, RUQ pain, tenderness or mass), systemic signs (fever, raised C-reactive protein (CRP) or white cells) and imaging findings.
Dysfunction of any organ: hypotension needing catecholamines; PaO2/FiO2 below 300; creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL; reduced consciousness; INR above 1.5; platelets below 100,000/µL.
Any of: symptoms over 72 hours; palpable RUQ mass; white cells above 18,000/µL; marked local inflammation (gangrenous cholecystitis).
Healthy patient with mild gallbladder inflammation and no Grade II or III features.

Absolute: suspected malignancy, polyp over 1 cm, porcelain gallbladder, chronic haemolytic anaemia, transplant patient, stones over 3 cm, multiple small stones, children. Relative: stones over 2 cm, stones under 3 mm with patent cystic duct, diabetes, non-functioning gallbladder.

pathophysiology.summary: Diabetic foot disease results from peripheral neuropathy, peripheral artery disease (PAD) and deformity, which together let unnoticed trauma become an ulcer. Loss of protective sensation (LOPS) removes the warning of pain; PAD impairs healing; infection spreads along tissue planes and to bone. Infection is diagnosed clinically and graded by severity (IWGDF/IDSA), which sets the antibiotic route, spectrum and need for surgery. Antibiotics do not work without wound care, debridement, offloading and good glucose control (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Sensory neuropathy removes protective pain; motor neuropathy causes deformity and high-pressure areas.
Peripheral artery disease reduces oxygen and antibiotic delivery to the wound.
Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function and healing.
Infection tracks into deep spaces, tendons and bone (osteomyelitis).

symptoms: Tingling, numbness, feeling of walking on a mattress (ICMR STW)
Intermittent claudication or rest pain (ICMR STW)
Wound, swelling, discharge, foul smell
physicalSigns: Loss of sensation to 10 g monofilament (ICMR STW)
Absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses (ICMR STW)
Deformity: hammer or claw toes, hallux valgus, pes cavus, rocker-bottom foot (ICMR STW)
Swelling, erythema, warmth, tenderness, pus (local infection signs)
redFlags: Sick, drowsy, abnormal breathing or pulse, fever (ICMR STW)
SIRS: two or more of temperature above 38°C or below 36°C, heart rate above 90/min, respiratory rate above 20/min, white cells above 12,000 or below 4,000/µL or over 10% bands (ICMR STW; IWGDF)
Gangrene, rest pain, osteomyelitis, acute Charcot foot (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Uncontrolled hyperglycaemia, long diabetes duration (ICMR STW)
Callus, prior ulcer or amputation (ICMR STW)
Visual impairment, chronic kidney disease (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Hot, swollen, red foot with intact skin and often little pain; refer (ICMR STW).
Absent pulses, ABI below 0.9, painful ulcer on toes or heel (ICMR STW).
Acute first-toe joint inflammation without a wound.
Calf swelling and tenderness without a foot wound.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: As printed in the STW: low risk (callus alone, no LOPS or PAD) — yearly; medium risk (previous amputation or ulceration plus any two of deformity, LOPS, PAD) — 6-monthly; high risk (deformity with LOPS or PAD) — 3-monthly.
Grade 1 uninfected; Grade 2 mild: at least two local signs (swelling or induration, erythema 0.5 to under 2 cm, tenderness, warmth, pus), skin and subcutaneous tissue only, no systemic signs.
Grade 3 moderate: erythema 2 cm or more or deeper than subcutaneous tissue, no systemic signs. Grade 4 severe: with two or more SIRS criteria. Add (O) if bone is involved.
ABI below 0.9: refer for evaluation and possible revascularisation.
Soft tissue 1–2 weeks (up to 3–4 weeks if slow healing or severe PAD); osteomyelitis 6 weeks without resection; 3 weeks after minor amputation with positive bone margin.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Not felt at one or more sites
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms LOPS; sets risk category (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Urinary stones form when urine is supersaturated with calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, uric acid or cystine. A stone moving into the ureter causes obstruction, ureteric spasm and capsular stretch, producing colicky loin pain that radiates according to the level of the stone (ICMR STW). Most small distal stones pass; larger stones and those with infection, obstruction of a solitary kidney, anuria or renal failure need urgent urological care. An obstructed, infected kidney is a urological emergency that needs drainage as well as antibiotics (BAUS).
keyMechanisms: Supersaturation, low urine volume and low citrate drive crystal formation.
Ureteric obstruction raises pressure in the collecting system, causing colic and hydronephrosis.
Pain radiates from flank to groin, thigh, scrotum or vulva as the stone descends (ICMR STW).
Infection behind an obstruction causes pyonephrosis and urosepsis.

pathophysiology.summary: Alcohol use disorder ranges from hazardous or harmful use to dependence. The ICMR workflow defines dependence as three of six features for at least one month: compulsion to drink, impaired control, withdrawal, tolerance, preoccupation, and continued use despite harm. Chronic alcohol enhances gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) and blocks N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors; when drinking stops, the brain is left hyperexcitable, causing tremor, sweating, anxiety, insomnia, seizures and delirium tremens. Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy, which can be precipitated by glucose. Treatment is benzodiazepine-covered withdrawal, thiamine, then relapse prevention with counselling and medicines.
keyMechanisms: Long-term alcohol up-regulates excitatory NMDA and down-regulates inhibitory GABA-A signalling.
Stopping alcohol unmasks hyperexcitability: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, seizures, delirium tremens.
Poor intake and absorption cause thiamine deficiency and Wernicke encephalopathy.
Craving and cue-driven reward learning drive relapse.

Amitriptyline for migraine prevention (NICE 1.3.18) uses the ICMR tension-type headache starting dose; a migraine-specific titration was not opened.

pathophysiology.summary: Headache is primary (migraine, tension-type, cluster and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias) or secondary to another disease such as subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, cerebral venous thrombosis or a space-occupying lesion. The first task is to look for red flags that point to a secondary cause (ICMR STW; NICE). Migraine involves trigeminovascular activation with release of vasoactive peptides, causing throbbing pain with nausea and light or sound sensitivity; cluster headache causes short, severe orbital pain with autonomic features. Overuse of acute medicines can itself cause daily headache.
keyMechanisms: Migraine: cortical and brainstem changes activate trigeminal nerves and release vasoactive peptides, causing throbbing pain.
Cluster headache: hypothalamic activation drives trigeminal-autonomic reflexes (tearing, red eye, nasal blockage).
Tension-type headache: pericranial muscle tenderness and central sensitisation.
Secondary headache: bleeding, raised pressure, inflammation or venous thrombosis stretch pain-sensitive structures.

symptoms: Migraine: side-alternating headache with visual aura, light and sound sensitivity, nausea; relieved by sleep or analgesics (ICMR STW)
Chronic tension-type: continuous bilateral headache for years with insomnia (ICMR STW)
Cluster: rapid-onset periorbital and temporal pain with autonomic features (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Usually normal neurological examination in primary headache
Tearing, red eye, ptosis in cluster headache
Fever, neck stiffness, papilloedema or focal signs suggest a secondary cause
redFlags: Thunderclap: sudden onset, maximal within seconds to minutes (ICMR STW)
First or worst headache of life (ICMR STW)
Headache with fever, neck stiffness, altered consciousness, personality change (ICMR STW)
New severe headache in pregnancy, postpartum or on hormones (ICMR STW)
New headache with cancer or immunosuppression; focal neurological signs; headache waking from sleep (ICMR STW)
Headache triggered by cough, Valsalva, exercise or posture; recent head trauma (NICE 1.1.1)
precipitants: Poor sleep, missed meals, migraine triggers (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Thunderclap onset; computed tomography (CT) angiogram, then cerebrospinal fluid if CT is negative (ICMR STW).
Fever, neck stiffness, altered sensorium; CT then cerebrospinal fluid study (ICMR STW).
Continuous headache, often postpartum or on hormones; magnetic resonance (MR) venogram (ICMR STW).
Progressive headache with seizures or focal deficit; contrast CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Red flags first
actions: Check every red flag; any danger sign means immediate referral and investigation (ICMR STW).
Image by presentation: CT or MRI with angiography for sudden or continuous headache; CT then cerebrospinal fluid for fever or altered sensorium (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Migraine attack
actions: Paracetamol 650 mg or indomethacin 50 mg, with prochlorperazine 10 mg for nausea (ICMR STW).
If simple analgesia fails: oral triptan combined with a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or paracetamol (NICE 1.3.10).
Do not offer ergots or opioids (NICE 1.3.14).

clinicalManagement.title: Migraine prevention
actions: Propranolol or flunarizine for a 2-month trial (ICMR STW); NICE offers topiramate or propranolol, or amitriptyline (NICE 1.3.17–1.3.18).
Review need 6 months after starting (NICE 1.3.22); taper after remission (ICMR STW).
Sleep at least 6 hours, regular meals, avoid triggers (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Tension-type headache
actions: Acute: aspirin, paracetamol or an NSAID; no opioids (NICE 1.3.7–1.3.8).
Chronic tension-type: indomethacin for 7 days, amitriptyline at bedtime (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Cluster headache
actions: 100% oxygen at 12 L/min or more by non-rebreathing mask, and/or subcutaneous triptan (NICE 1.3.29–1.3.30).
Do not give paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots or oral triptans (NICE 1.3.32).
Refer to a tertiary centre (ICMR STW); verapamil prevention under specialist advice (NICE 1.3.33).

clinicalManagement.title: Medication overuse
actions: Withdraw overused medicines abruptly for at least 1 month; warn of temporary worsening; review in 4–8 weeks (NICE 1.3.37–1.3.42).
